issues.legal_issue: A pre-Constitution allotment order cannot be invalidated under fundamental rights guarantees that came into force later merely because physical possession was taken after those guarantees came into force.
material_facts: The house became vacant and was allotted to another occupant before the Constitution came into force.
Under the allotment order, the owner was required to deliver possession and had lost the right to possess the house.
Physical possession was taken after the Constitution came into force, pursuant to a later enforcement order.
issues.conclusion: The allotment order could not be challenged under Articles 31(2) or 19(1)(f); the later taking of physical possession did not change that result.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 13(1), an earlier law and rights and liabilities accrued under it remain operative for past transactions. Keshavan Madhava Menon v. The State of Bombay, [1951] SCR 228, establishes that a law inconsistent with fundamental rights is not rendered void for transactions predating the Constitution. Because the allotment order had already ended the owner's right to possession, later enforcement was only a consequence of that order.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_allocati: A person brings a constitutional writ challenging an official allocation of property.
predicates.allocation_order_preceded_fundamental_ri: The official allocation order was made before the relevant fundamental rights guarantees came into force.
predicates.owner_lost_possession_right_under_alloca: The allocation order ended the owner's right to possess the property before physical enforcement occurred.
predicates.physical_possession_taken_later: Officials took physical possession after the relevant fundamental rights guarantees came into force.
predicates.pre_guarantee_allocation_not_invalidated: An allocation made before fundamental rights guarantees came into force is not invalidated under those guarantees merely because it is enforced later.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges an allocation made before fundamental rights guarantees came into force, and the allocation had already ended the owner's possession right before later physical enforcement, the earlier allocation is not invalidated by a later fundamental-rights claim.

issues.legal_issue: Physical possession taken to enforce an allotment is not an acquisition by the State from the owner when the allotment had already ended the owner's entitlement to possession.
material_facts: The allotment order required the owner to give possession to the allottee and treated the allottee as the tenant.
The owner did not surrender possession, and officials later took possession under an enforcement order and delivered it to the allottee.
issues.conclusion: Article 31(2) did not apply because there was no acquisition by the State; the owner had already lost the right to possession under the allotment order.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) concerns acquisition by the State. The Court reasoned that possession can be taken from a person entitled to possession, but the allotment order had already ended the owner's entitlement. The Control Order's allotment and tenancy provisions therefore meant the subsequent taking of possession was not an acquisition from the owner by the State.

predicates.constitutional_property_claim_challengin: A person brings a constitutional property claim challenging officials' taking of possession.
predicates.allocation_order_ended_owner_possession_: An allocation order ended the owner's entitlement to possess the property before officials physically took it.
predicates.officials_later_enforced_allocation: Officials later took possession to carry out the allocation and delivered the property to the allottee.
predicates.later_enforcement_not_acquisition_from_o: Later enforcement of the allocation is not an acquisition by the State from the former owner.

issues.definition: If an allocation has already ended the owner's entitlement to possession before officials enforce it, the later enforcement is not an acquisition from that owner.

issues.legal_issue: The power to regulate the letting and subletting of accommodation is not limited to accommodation that the owner has made available for letting.
material_facts: The house became vacant, and the owner notified the Controller that he wanted it for his own use in establishing his son in business.
The Controller allotted the house for the occupation of a private individual associated with a children's school.
The allotment was made under the amended Control Order, which permitted allocation for an individual's occupation.
issues.conclusion: The power under Rule 81(2)(bb) of the Defence of India Rules was not confined to cases where the house was available for letting or subletting in the sense that the owner did not require it for personal use or had not already let it.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 81(2)(bb) of the Defence of India Rules empowered the authorities to regulate the letting and subletting of accommodation, including by requiring accommodation to be let to specified persons or classes. Read in light of that purpose, the power was not restricted to accommodation an owner had chosen to make available for letting; such a restriction would allow the regulatory power to be avoided by an assertion of personal use or an existing letting. The Court also noted that the Control Order had been made under an additional enactment whose text was not before it, and did not decide a challenge to the amendment on that basis.

predicates.challenge_to_accommodation_allocation_po: A proceeding challenges the authority to allocate accommodation under a scheme regulating its letting.
predicates.accommodation_owner_claimed_for_personal: The owner claimed that the accommodation was required for the owner's own use rather than being offered for rent.
predicates.authority_allocated_accommodation_to_ano: The authority allocated the accommodation to another occupant despite the owner's claim of personal use.
predicates.regulatory_power_not_limited_to_accommod: The power to regulate letting is not confined to accommodation that the owner has made available for rent.

issues.definition: When an allocation-power challenge concerns accommodation the owner claims for personal use but the authority allocates to another occupant, the regulatory power is not limited to accommodation offered for rent.
